title: How Google Maps knows there’s traffic
musicPrompt: Calm, curious lo-fi electronic bed for an 86-second explainer, about 90 BPM, soft plucked synth arpeggio, warm sub bass, light clock-like hi-hats, a lift when the road turns into dots and lines around 45 seconds and a gentle resolve in the last 10 seconds, instrumental, no vocals.

scenes.text: How does Google Maps know about a traffic jam before you even reach it?
Welcome to How It Scales, by Curiously.
In 2020, an artist in Berlin pulled ninety-nine second-hand phones through the streets in a handcart. On Google Maps, those streets turned red.
Google pools location data from lots of people's phones. When lots of them crawl along one road, Google can tell it's slow.
But you need to know the traffic ten, twenty, even fifty minutes into your drive.
So Google also remembers how each road usually flows, and mixes that with live traffic.
To forecast, Google teamed up with DeepMind, an Alphabet AI lab, on a graph neural network. Picture every stretch of road as a dot, with lines joining stretches that connect.
Neighbouring dots pass messages to each other, so the model learns how a jam on a side street spills onto a bigger road.
In 2020, Google said its arrival time predictions were accurate for over ninety-seven percent of trips.
So before you get there, phones already stuck in the jam have helped tell Google. Even phones in a handcart.
